title: Assortment planning: breadth, depth, and store clusters
summary: Assortment planning sets which products each store carries and how deep. See the breadth vs depth math, store clusters, and what 50 experiments say on choice.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 20 November 2026.


Assortment planning is the process of deciding which products each store or channel will carry, in how many variants, and in what depth, for a given period and budget. It sits between the financial plan, which says how much you can buy, and allocation, which sends the units to each location.


Every choice in assortment planning has a cost in the same currency. A wider range means fewer units behind each product, and a deeper buy means fewer products on the wall. Buyers know the trade-off by instinct, but it is rarely put into numbers before the orders are placed.


This guide puts numbers on assortment planning with one retailer followed from start to finish: the breadth versus depth calculation, store clustering, a six-step process, and the places where the method misleads. If you would rather test it on your own categories, you can[review your range with our team](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


**Key Takeaways**


- Assortment planning decides which products each store carries, in how many variants, and how deep. Breadth and depth are paid from the same budget.
- In the worked example, a store that buys 500 pairs gets 16.7 pairs per option with 30 options and 27.8 pairs with 18 options.
- In Iyengar and Lepper's field experiment (2000), a display of 24 jams stopped 60% of passers-by against 40% for 6 jams, yet nearly 30% of those who stopped at the small display bought, against 3% at the large one.
- A 2010 meta-analysis of 50 choice experiments with 5,036 participants found a mean effect of "virtually zero", so assortment planning has to measure the right range size category by category.
- Three store clusters cut the example plan from 1,080 store and option combinations to 784, and average depth rises from 20.0 to 27.6 pairs.


## What is assortment planning?


Assortment planning is the retail process that selects the products offered in each store and channel for a season or a period. It fixes the number of categories and products (breadth), the number of variants and units behind each product (depth), and the differences between locations. The aim is the mix that sells best within a fixed budget and a fixed amount of shelf room.


Some teams call it range planning. The vocabulary also shifts between sectors, so it helps to fix three terms for the rest of this article. An option is one product in one color, a variant is one size of that option, and depth is the number of units bought per option.


Assortment planning is often confused with the two plans on either side of it. The table shows what each one decides.


Plan Question it answers Unit of work Typical owner


Merchandise financial plan How much can we buy, by category and month? Value at cost or retail Merchandise planner


Assortment plan Which options, how many, how deep, in which stores? Options and units by store cluster Buyer and planner together


Allocation How many units of each variant go to each store, and when? Units by variant and store Allocator


The financial plan comes first, and our guide to[open-to-buy planning](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/open-to-buy-planning) covers how that budget is built. The assortment plan spends it, then allocation executes it.


## Breadth vs depth: the trade-off at the center of assortment planning


Breadth and depth compete for the same units, and that competition is the first thing assortment planning has to settle. The easiest way to see it is to hold the budget fixed and change only the number of options.


Take a sports and outdoor retailer with 36 stores and its trail running shoe category (an illustrative example with our own arithmetic, reused in every section). A standard store has a season buy of 500 pairs for the category. Each option comes in 10 sizes.


Lucia, the category buyer, compared two drafts for that store (an illustrative case). The first carried 30 options and the second 18.


Broad draft Focused draft


Options in the store 30 18


Season buy (pairs) 500 500


Pairs per option 16.7 27.8


Pairs in a core size (16% of sales) 2.7 4.4


Pairs in an edge size (4% of sales) 0.7 1.1


In this category, the two middle sizes each account for about 16% of sales and the smallest and largest for about 4% each. With 30 options, a core size has fewer than three pairs for the whole season. The second sale in that size leaves one pair, and the option is effectively broken for the customers most likely to buy it.


The edge sizes show the other half of the problem. A store cannot stock 0.7 of a pair, so the buyer rounds up to one and overbuys, or rounds down to zero and leaves a gap. In the focused draft each size gets at least one full pair without rounding up.


Lucia did not conclude that fewer options is always better. The broad draft offered 12 more options, and some customers would have bought one of those and nothing else. What the table gave her was the price of those 12 extra options: 1.7 pairs fewer in each core size of every option in the store.


### Depth follows the size curve


Depth per option only makes sense once it is split by variant, a step that assortment planning done at option level tends to skip. The split, often called the size curve, should come from sales in that category and that group of stores, corrected for the weeks when a size was out of stock. A curve copied from the national average puts too many small sizes in some stores and too few in others.


The same reasoning applies outside footwear. In beauty the variants are shades, in furniture they are fabrics and finishes, and in tableware they are colors of the same plate. Wherever a product has variants, breadth multiplies the number of stock positions faster than it looks on the range plan, so assortment planning has to count variants as well as options.


## How much choice do customers want? What the research says


The usual argument in assortment planning for a narrower range is that too much choice puts customers off. The evidence is more mixed than that argument suggests, and it is worth knowing before you cut.


The best-known study is a field experiment by Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 2000. A tasting booth in a California grocery store displayed either 24 jams or 6. The large display stopped 60% of passers-by (145 of 242) and the small one 40% (104 of 260).


Purchases went the other way. Nearly 30% of the shoppers who stopped at the 6-jam display bought a jar, against 3% at the 24-jam display. The large range attracted more people and converted far fewer of them.


Later work complicates the picture. In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne, Rainer Greifeneder, and Peter Todd pooled 63 conditions from 50 experiments, covering 5,036 participants, in the Journal of Consumer Research. They found a mean effect size of "virtually zero" with considerable variance between studies. Sometimes more choice reduced purchases and sometimes it raised them.


Evidence from real range cuts points the same way. A 2005 study in Marketing Science by Sharad Borle and co-authors followed customers of an online grocer after a large assortment reduction. Shopping frequency and purchase quantity both fell, and the effect varied widely by category, with less frequently purchased categories hit harder.


For assortment planning, the practical reading is that no universal number of options exists. A large range draws traffic, a small one can convert better, and the balance depends on the category and on how easily customers switch between options. That is a reason to measure the effect in your own sales data before deciding how far to cut.


## Store clustering: one assortment plan per group of stores


A single range for every store is easy to manage and wrong for most of them. One range per store is accurate and impossible to buy or to run. Store clustering is the compromise most assortment planning relies on: stores are grouped by how their customers buy, and each group gets its own version of the plan.


### Cluster on demand as well as size


The common starting point is sales volume, because large stores can hold more options. Volume is necessary, and it does not capture what customers in a given store actually choose.


Mateo, the retailer's merchandise planner, compared two stores that each sold about 520 pairs of trail shoes last season (an illustrative case). In the store on the edge of a large city, 68% of pairs were light models priced under €130. In the store in a mountain valley, 61% were waterproof or heavily cushioned models priced above €150.


The two stores were twins by volume and needed different ranges, since a shared plan would have left the city store with technical shoes it could not sell and the valley store short of them. Mateo built the clusters on three inputs: category volume, the share of sales by product attribute, and price band.


### What three clusters change


He ended with three clusters for the category. Twelve core options go to all 36 stores, and each cluster adds its own.


Cluster Stores Season buy per store (pairs) Options Pairs per option


City flagship 8 900 30 30.0


Standard 18 500 18 27.8


Mountain and resort 10 540 22 24.5


The total buy is 21,600 pairs. If all 36 stores carried the flagship range of 30 options, the plan would contain 1,080 store and option combinations at an average of 20.0 pairs each. The clustered plan contains 784 combinations at an average of 27.6 pairs.


Nothing was added to the budget. The same pairs were concentrated on the options each cluster sells, which is the whole purpose of a localized assortment. Our article on[tiered stock allocation](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/smarter-stock-allocation-to-maximize-full-price-sales) covers the next step, when those units are split between the stores of a cluster.


Across Metreecs' work with multi-store retailers, clusters built once and reused for every category are a recurring source of misfit. A store can be a flagship for running shoes and an average store for camping equipment. Clustering by category adds work at the start of assortment planning and saves markdowns later.


## The assortment planning process in six steps


This assortment planning sequence works for a seasonal category and for a permanent one. Only the review frequency changes.


1. **Set the role and budget of the category.** Start from the financial plan: the buy at cost, the planned margin, and the room available in each store format. A category meant to bring traffic is planned wider than one meant to earn margin.
2. **Analyze past demand by attribute.** Look at sales by price band, color family, material, and function, and correct them for stockouts. Attributes show what customers were choosing between, which a list of last year's best sellers does not.
3. **Build the store clusters.** Group stores by category volume and by attribute mix, as in the example above. Keep the number of clusters small enough to buy and to merchandise, which usually means three to five per category.
4. **Design the range architecture.** Fix the number of options per cluster, then divide them into core options carried everywhere, cluster options, and a small share reserved for tests. Check each proposed option against the attributes already covered, so that two options do not compete for the same customer.
5. **Set depth by option and by variant.** Forecast demand for each option in each cluster, then apply the size curve and the minimum display quantity. For options with no history, our guide to[forecasting new products without sales history](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/new-product-forecasting-without-sales-history) explains how to borrow demand from comparable products.
6. **Review in season.** Compare sales and stock by option with the plan after the first weeks, then decide what to reorder, what to stop, and what to move.


Step 6 is where assortment planning meets real sales, and much of the margin is decided there. Hana runs the in-season review for the same retailer (an illustrative case). In week 6 of a 26-week season, the bottom eight options in the flagship cluster had produced 6% of the pairs sold while holding 21% of the category stock.


She cancelled the open reorders on those eight options. The budget went to the five best sellers, whose core sizes were already missing in 11 of the 36 stores. Classifying options by contribution and by regularity of demand, as described in our guide to[ABC XYZ analysis](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/abc-xyz-analysis) , gives this review a consistent basis from one season to the next.


## Where assortment planning goes wrong


Four situations produce assortment planning that looks reasoned and still misses. Each has a structural cause that can be checked in the data.


### Sales history only shows what was stocked


Past sales measure demand for the products a store carried, during the weeks it had them. A store that never received waterproof models shows no demand for them. One mistake we repeatedly see is a cluster definition built on raw sales, which sends each store more of what it already had and confirms last year's plan.


Correcting for stockouts helps for products that were ranged. For products that were never ranged in a store, the estimate has to come from comparable stores in which they were available.


### Substitution is ignored


When assortment planning removes an option, part of its demand moves to a neighboring option and part is lost. The share that transfers decides whether the cut pays. Two near-identical grey shoes at the same price substitute well, while the only wide-fit model in the range does not.


The buyers we work with often underestimate how much of a slow option's demand comes from customers who would buy nothing else. This is consistent with the Marketing Science study cited above, in which the categories bought least often suffered most from the cut. A low-selling option that is the only one of its kind deserves a different test from a low-selling duplicate.


### The average hides the variants


An option can show a healthy sell-through while its core sizes have been out of stock for weeks. The remaining stock is in the edge sizes, which will be marked down. Any review done at option level should include a count of stores in which the core variants are missing.


### Demand per variant and store is very small


In the standard store, 500 pairs over 26 weeks is about 19 pairs a week for the whole category. Spread across 18 options and 10 sizes, most variants sell less than one pair a month in a given store. Hand-built assortment planning copes by averaging across stores, which removes the local differences the clusters were meant to capture.


This is where a demand forecast for each product in each location earns its place, because it gives depth and size decisions a number per store. That forecast is what Metreecs produces with AI-powered[demand planning](https://www.metreecs.com/demand-planning) , including for new products matched to comparable ones. Assortment planning decisions stay with the buyer, who knows what the brand should stand for.


## FAQ


### What is the difference between assortment planning and merchandise planning?


Merchandise planning sets the financial frame: sales, margin, stock, and purchase budget by category and month. Assortment planning works inside that frame and decides which options to buy, how deep, and for which stores. A retailer needs both, with merchandise planning first and assortment planning second.


### What do breadth and depth mean in a retail assortment?


Breadth is the number of different categories or products a retailer offers. Depth is the number of variants and units behind each product. With a fixed budget, adding breadth reduces depth, as in the worked example where going from 18 to 30 options cut the buy from 27.8 to 16.7 pairs per option.


### How many store clusters should assortment planning use?


Most retailers work with three to five clusters per category. Fewer than three usually means stores with different demand share a range. More than five becomes hard to buy and to merchandise, and each cluster has too little sales history to plan from.


### How often should an assortment plan be reviewed?


For seasonal categories, review after the first three to six weeks of sales and again at mid-season, while reorders and transfers are still possible. For permanent ranges, a quarterly review of the slowest and fastest options is a reasonable rhythm. The review should look at variants as well as options.


### Does reducing the number of products increase sales?


It can, and it can also reduce them. Controlled experiments on choice show effects in both directions, and a 2010 meta-analysis of 50 experiments found an average effect close to zero. The outcome depends on whether customers find a substitute in what remains, which varies by category and is why assortment planning should test a cut before rolling it out.


## Conclusion


Assortment planning comes down to spending a fixed budget on the right options for each group of stores, with enough depth for every option to stay complete in its core variants. Put numbers on breadth versus depth before buying, build clusters on what customers choose in each category, and review by variant during the season.
